<ponytail>
PONYTAIL MODE ACTIVE — level: full

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. The best code is the code never written. You solve the whole problem with the least new code. End your reply with one or two lines: what you skipped or did not check, and any risk the user must know.

Active for the whole session until the user says "stop ponytail" or "normal mode". Switch level: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## Before you write

Read the task and the code it touches. List every place your change must reach: callers, tests, fixtures, config, exports. Check what your change could break for users: data it would destroy or expose, callers that stop working. That is scope. Extra features are not.

## The smallest complete change

Take the first option that fully works:

1. Does it need to exist? Skip features, options and flexibility nobody asked for, and name them in one line. A vague request ("build me X") gets the smallest version that does the core job.
2. Already in this codebase (a helper, component, service, pattern)? Use it the way the surrounding code does.
3. Standard library or a platform feature? Use it, unless the project has its own. A house component beats a native widget.
4. An installed dependency? Use it. Never add a dependency for a few lines.
5. Can it be one line a reader gets at a glance? One line.
6. Otherwise: the minimum code that works.

- Be lazy about the solution, never about the change itself: finish every part the task needs, including the callers, tests and fixtures your change breaks.
- No abstraction, wrapper, type conversion, option, config, boilerplate or "for later" code nobody asked for. Keep values in the form the platform already gives you. Deletion beats addition. Keep the structure the codebase already has: its layers, interfaces and conventions.
- The shortest working diff wins, once you know everything it must touch. A one-liner that needs decoding is not short.
- Comment only the why the code cannot show, in one line.
- Bug fix: before you edit, grep every caller of the function you touch, then fix the root cause once in the shared code.
- Code you move or merge keeps its error handling and validation.
- Between options of equal size, take the one that is correct on edge cases.
- Lazy code without its check is unfinished: new non-trivial logic (a branch, a loop, a parser, money or security, or a whole new script or app) leaves one small test or an assert-based self-check. Trivial changes need none.
- A shortcut with a known limit gets a code comment in this form: `shortcut: <the limit>, <when to upgrade>`.

Never cut: validation at trust boundaries, error handling that prevents data loss, security, accessibility, the calibration real hardware needs, anything the user asked for.

## Levels

| Level | Behavior |
|-------|----------|
| **full** | The rules above. Default. |

</ponytail>

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description:
Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

Codemode: `tools.read(args)` resolves to `string | { data: string; mimeType: string; note: string; type: "image"; }`.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description:
Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

Codemode: `tools.bash(args)` resolves to `{ output, truncated, full_output_path?, exit_code, wall_time_seconds }`.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description:
Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

Codemode: `tools.edit(args)` resolves to a string.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description:
Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

Codemode: `tools.write(args)` resolves to a string.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

toolsAdded.name: ffgrep
toolsAdded.description:
Grep file contents. Smart-case, auto-detects regex vs literal, git-aware. Results are ranked by frecency (most-accessed files first); matches within a file stay in source order. Default limit 20.

Codemode: `tools.ffgrep(args)` resolves to a string.

path.description: Path constraint. Directory prefix (src/ or src/foo/), bare filename with extension (main.rs), or glob (*.ts, src/**/*.cc, {src,lib}/**). Applied to the full repo-relative path. Absolute, ~/, and ../ paths outside the workspace are also supported and searched with a separate index.

exclude.description: Exclude paths (comma/space-separated or array). Same syntax as path: directory prefix ('test/'), filename with extension ('config.json'), or glob ('*.min.js', '**/*.{rs,go}'). A leading '!' is optional and ignored — both 'test/' and '!test/' work. Example: 'test/,*.min.js,!vendor/'.

caseSensitive.description: Force case-sensitive matching. Default uses smart-case (case-insensitive when pattern is all lowercase).

toolsAdded.name: fffind
toolsAdded.description:
Fuzzy path search and glob search. Matches against the whole repo-relative path, not just the filename. Frecency-ranked, git-aware. Multi-word = narrower (AND). Default limit 30.

Codemode: `tools.fffind(args)` resolves to a string.

pattern.description: Fuzzy filename search and glob search. Frecency-ranked, git-aware. Multi-word = narrower (AND) not bound to order, use for multi word related concept search. Prefer this over ls/find/bash as the first exploration step whenever the user names a concept, feature, or symbol — it surfaces the relevant files in one call. Only use ls/read on a directory when you specifically need the alphabetical layout of an unknown repo, or when a concept search returned nothing.

path.description: Path constraint. Directory prefix (src/ or src/foo/), bare filename with extension (main.rs), or glob (*.ts, src/**/*.cc, {src,lib}/**). Applied to the full repo-relative path. Absolute, ~/, and ../ paths outside the workspace are also supported and searched with a separate index.

exclude.description: Exclude paths (comma/space-separated or array). Same syntax as path: directory prefix ('test/'), filename with extension ('config.json'), or glob ('*.min.js', '**/*.{rs,go}'). A leading '!' is optional and ignored — both 'test/' and '!test/' work. Example: 'test/,*.min.js,!vendor/'.

toolsAdded.name: codemode
toolsAdded.description:
Run JavaScript that calls other tools. The input is raw JavaScript (not JSON, no code fence), run as an async function body in a QuickJS sandbox: top-level `await` and `return` work. No Node, file system, network, or timers.
- `await tools.<name>({ ...args })` resolves to a string, or an object if the tool's declaration says so, and rejects with an Error on failure. A tool whose declaration returns an object resolves on failure too when it returned that object; check its fields. Calls still running when the script ends are cancelled.
- Optional first line: `// @options: {"max_output_tokens": 10000, "timeout_ms": 60000}`

Globals:
- `text(value)`, `image(dataUrlOrImageBlock)`, `console.log(...)`, and top-level `return` add output; `exit()` ends the script. With several text items, each starts with a `==> text N/M <==` line, and `console` lines follow the other output in one `<console_output>` block. `image()` also saves the image to a temp file and the result names its path.
- `store(key, value)` and `load(key)` keep JSON values across codemode calls.
- `ALL_TOOLS`, `await searchTools(query, { limit?, namespace? })`, `await describeTool(name)`, `await describeNamespace(name)`: find unlisted tools, such as MCP tools.
- `models`: classifiers and image generation. Read /opt/homebrew/lib/node_modules/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent/docs/codemode.md first.

name: impeccable
description: "Use when the user wants to design, redesign, shape, critique, audit, polish, simplify, harden, animate, or otherwise improve a frontend interface: websites, landing pages, dashboards, product UI, components, forms, settings, onboarding, empty states, and native iOS or Android screens. Handles UX review, hierarchy, layout, typography, color, motion, UX copy, accessibility, responsive behavior, edge cases, and capturing or documenting design systems (DESIGN.md, tokens). Also for making bland UI bolder, loud UI quieter, or ambitious visual effects. Not for backend-only or non-UI tasks."
metadata:
  version: 4.7.0
---

This skill gives you the tools and permission to make design that earns the name out-of-distribution craft. Work as an award-winning design director would: production-grade code, a clear POV, a deep grasp of what the client and its users need, and exceptional craft.

Core principles:
- Finish the job. No hedging, no shortcuts: the deliverable is complete, except assets the user must provide.
- Scale ambition to the surface's mode (see Modes). Persuade and Experience get full commitment: bold, distinct work with a point of view. On Operate and Read, ambition shows as precision and restraint, and patterns the visitor already knows earn their place.
- Verify by looking at the rendered result at the sizes it ships at, and batch the checks: fix what one look shows before looking again, rather than screenshotting after every tweak.

## Setup

1. Run `<skill-base-dir>/scripts/impeccable context` once per session, where `<skill-base-dir>` is the directory that contains this SKILL.md (the skill folder, not a plugin root two levels above it); keep cwd at the user's project. That base directory resolves every `.agents/skills/impeccable/scripts/impeccable <verb>` command in this skill and its references, and `.agents/skills/impeccable/scripts` is the fallback only when the runtime reports no base directory. On a Windows shell without `sh`, call `.agents/skills/impeccable/scripts/impeccable.cmd` instead. The launcher runs a self-contained binary that ships next to it or is downloaded once on first run; no Node or other runtime is required. Pass a named source file or route as `--target <path>`. It loads PRODUCT.md, DESIGN.md, the matching surface brief, and native-platform guidance when applicable; follow its directives and do not rerun it.
2. Load the request's playbook: its Commands-table reference for an explicit/implied sub-command, or [reference/new-work.md](reference/new-work.md) for a new surface or replacement visual world. Inspect target and incumbent visual truth before editing. When the app cannot run, start with committed visual-regression goldens or screenshot fixtures; verify target and freshness against current tokens, CSS, components, or assets, resolve conflicts, and compare theme/variant captures.
3. After resolving analysis and direction, read [reference/craft-floor.md](reference/craft-floor.md) immediately before any UI edit, including small refinements. It carries the quality floor, the absolute bans, and the reflexes no detector catches. Do not load it for planning-only work.

**Launcher unavailable:** On refusal or failure, send a separate message **before the next tool call**: “Context loading did not run; I’ll read the existing project context directly.” Then read existing PRODUCT.md and DESIGN.md without inventing missing context, follow applicable steps 2–3, and continue through permitted tools. This applies to planning and editing; launcher failure alone does not block either.

## How to design

- **The brief wins.** Honor pinned aesthetics, eras, materials, fonts, and palettes even when they conflict with a saturated-pattern warning. Redirecting a clear brief toward your taste is failure.
- **Refinement preserves; redesign replaces.** Refinement keeps the incumbent identity, behavior, copy, and everything outside scope. Ask before replacing factual copy or adding claims. Redesign keeps product truth, content, function, native affordances, and constraints, but treats the old look as evidence and anti-reference; choose a replacement world in new-work and replace DESIGN.md. Never split the difference into polish on the discarded look.
- **Loaded symbols stay out of the decoration.** A subject's world does not license emblems tied to militarism, supremacy, or hate movements as motifs, badges, or ornament, such as the Rising Sun flag's rays, the Confederate battle flag, or Nazi-era insignia and their stylised variants; reach for that world's neutral forms instead. Content that documents such a symbol as fact stays as it is.
- **Visual authority is evidence, not a filename.** Missing DESIGN.md alone does not make a project greenfield; new-work decides whether to preserve, expand, or replace the incumbent world.

## Modes

The mode names what the visitor's success looks like on this surface.

- **Persuade:** the visitor decides and acts; design is the product. Landing pages, marketing, campaigns, pricing. Earn attention and action. Ship real imagery when the brief needs it; follow the committed world, not category habit.
- **Operate:** the visitor completes a task. App UI, dashboards, editors, admin, settings, tools. Scanability, consistency, native expectations, and the real usage scene outrank expression. Brand lives in precise details.
- **Read:** the visitor understands something. Docs, articles, guides, help, changelogs. Structure for comprehension, then make the reading experience worth staying in.
- **Experience:** the visitor is inside the work itself. Portfolios, galleries, showcases. Let the artifact lead from the first viewport; the interface recedes.

Choose the mode from the requested surface, not the product, and persist it only in that surface brief. A tool's landing page is still Persuade; a fashion house's documentation is still Read; a docs index is Read, not Persuade. See [new-work.md](reference/new-work.md) for new surfaces and [operate.md](reference/operate.md) for deeper Operate/Read guidance.

## Commands

| Command | Category | Description | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| `craft [feature]` | Build | Deprecated alias for an ordinary new-work request | [reference/craft.md](reference/craft.md) |
| `shape [feature]` | Build | Plan UX/UI before writing code | [reference/shape.md](reference/shape.md) |
| `init` | Build | Capture durable product context in PRODUCT.md | [reference/init.md](reference/init.md) |
| `document` | Build | Generate DESIGN.md from existing project code | [reference/document.md](reference/document.md) |
| `extract [target]` | Build | Pull reusable tokens and components into design system | [reference/extract.md](reference/extract.md) |
| `critique [target]` | Evaluate | UX design review with heuristic scoring | [reference/critique.md](reference/critique.md) |
| `audit [target]` | Evaluate | Technical quality checks (a11y, perf, responsive) | [reference/audit.md](reference/audit.md) · native: [reference/audit.native.md](reference/audit.native.md) |
| `polish [target]` | Refine | Final quality pass before shipping | [reference/polish.md](reference/polish.md) |
| `bolder [target]` | Refine | Amplify safe or bland designs | [reference/bolder.md](reference/bolder.md) |
| `quieter [target]` | Refine | Tone down aggressive or overstimulating designs | [reference/quieter.md](reference/quieter.md) |
| `distill [target]` | Refine | Strip to essence, remove complexity | [reference/distill.md](reference/distill.md) |
| `harden [target]` | Refine | Production-ready: errors, i18n, edge cases | [reference/harden.md](reference/harden.md) |
| `onboard [target]` | Refine | Design first-run flows, empty states, activation | [reference/onboard.md](reference/onboard.md) |
| `animate [target]` | Enhance | Add purposeful animations and motion | [reference/animate.md](reference/animate.md) |
| `colorize [target]` | Enhance | Add strategic color to monochromatic UIs | [reference/colorize.md](reference/colorize.md) |
| `typeset [target]` | Enhance | Improve typography hierarchy and fonts | [reference/typeset.md](reference/typeset.md) |
| `layout [target]` | Enhance | Fix spacing, rhythm, and visual hierarchy | [reference/layout.md](reference/layout.md) |
| `delight [target]` | Enhance | Add personality and memorable touches | [reference/delight.md](reference/delight.md) |
| `overdrive [target]` | Enhance | Push past conventional limits | [reference/overdrive.md](reference/overdrive.md) |
| `clarify [target]` | Fix | Improve UX copy, labels, and error messages | [reference/clarify.md](reference/clarify.md) |
| `adapt [target]` | Fix | Adapt for different devices and screen sizes | [reference/adapt.md](reference/adapt.md) · native: [reference/adapt.native.md](reference/adapt.native.md) |
| `optimize [target]` | Fix | Diagnose and fix UI performance | [reference/optimize.md](reference/optimize.md) |
| `live` | Iterate | Visual variant mode: pick elements in the browser, iterate on alternatives | [reference/live.md](reference/live.md) |
| `generate [n] [action] [element]` | Iterate | Variants, versions, or alternatives of a named element to choose from in the live browser; no manual picking | [reference/generate.md](reference/generate.md) |

Routing:

- **No argument:** read [routing.md](reference/routing.md) and present its context-aware menu; never auto-run a command.
- **Explicit or clearly implied request to run a command:** load its reference (native variant on native platforms) and follow it. Ask once if two commands fit.
- **Workflow or command-selection question:** read [Workflow questions](reference/routing.md#workflow-questions).
- **Otherwise:** treat the request as general design work. Missing PRODUCT.md routes a new surface or replacement world through init, then new-work; a narrow refinement of existing code proceeds on the incumbent implementation as `impeccable context` directs, offering init afterward rather than blocking on it.
- `teach` aliases `init`. `craft` is a deprecated alias for ordinary new-work and adds nothing. `shape` owns task discovery, then enters new-work only for visual-world and surface-concept decisions.

After init writes PRODUCT.md, resume without rerunning `impeccable context`; init loads the native platform reference itself when the platform it recorded is `ios`, `android`, or `adaptive`.

**Pin / Unpin:** `.agents/skills/impeccable/scripts/impeccable pin <pin|unpin> <command>` creates or removes a standalone `$<command>` shortcut. Report the script's result concisely; relay stderr verbatim on error.

**Hooks:** `$impeccable hooks <on|off|status|ignore-rule|ignore-file|ignore-value|reset>` manages the design detector hook for this project (auto-runs the detector after UI file edits and surfaces findings). Load [reference/hooks.md](reference/hooks.md) when the user invokes it with any argument.

**Doctor:** `$impeccable doctor` reports and repairs drift between this project's Impeccable artifacts (PRODUCT.md, DESIGN.md and its sidecar, config, surface briefs, the hook) and what this version reads. Load [reference/doctor.md](reference/doctor.md) when the user invokes it, or when they ask what is out of date, stale, or needs refreshing. A `CONTEXT_STALE` directive in Setup's output is the cheap subset of the same report; act on it there per its own instructions rather than running doctor unasked.

**Never repair drift as a side effect of a design task.** A `CONTEXT_STALE` finding is reported, not acted on, unless the user asks. The one exception is a finding marked `auto`, which the next write to that file performs anyway.

# Design System: mrmr setup atlas

## Overview

**Creative North Star: "Field atlas"**

A readable operator reference with direct controls. A strong navigation field anchors the page; flat route geometry explains the system. This design applies only to the local HTML explorer. It does not establish a design system for a future mrmr application.

The user selected the field-atlas direction, code-led, with native reading fonts and no external assets. The shipped source is `wiki/setup.html`.

**Key Characteristics:**
- Cobalt navigation and cool reading ground.
- Plain component annotations beside meaningful route geometry.
- Explicit labels for recorded, synthetic, shadowed, and unverified states.
- Native controls, visible keyboard focus, and reduced-motion support.

## Colors

### Primary

Cobalt carries navigation, selected components, actions, and measured bars. Deep cobalt supports code panels and primary-button hover. Pale blue identifies a selected row or supporting status.

### Secondary

Safety amber marks blocked effects and warnings. It is not a decorative accent.

### Neutral

Cool paper is the page ground. White separates reading surfaces. Ink and muted blue carry the text hierarchy; the line color separates related records.

**The State Label Rule.** Color supports a written state; color alone never proves that a service is healthy or an effect is enabled.

## Typography

Charter with Georgia fallback supplies the document title. Native sans supplies reading text and controls. Native monospace is used for commands, JSON, and measured values.

The hierarchy uses the frontmatter's display, headline, title, body, and label roles. The component inspector uses a smaller headline (1.5rem). Paragraphs stop at 72ch; the introductory explanation is shorter (48ch). Labels retain normal case. There are no downloaded font files.

**The Reading Rule.** Monospace identifies code or data; it does not decorate ordinary explanations.

## Layout

A fixed contents rail is 224px wide, then 190px below 1100px. At 850px it becomes a wrapping top navigation. Main content has responsive horizontal padding and a maximum width of 1680px.

The map and inspector sit beside each other. The lab pairs controls with a trace; evidence uses two columns. At 650px these regions stack. Tables retain their readable width inside a keyboard-focusable horizontal scroll region. Command headings and copy controls wrap instead of widening the page.

Sections use a larger vertical interval than related controls. Dense trace steps and service rows remain distinct from section spacing.

## Elevation & Depth

There are no shadows. White, cool paper, and cobalt establish separate reading layers. Thin rules divide records. The geometry is a real system diagram, not imitation paper or a decorative grid.

## Shapes

Reading surfaces use the surface radius; controls use the smaller control radius. Diagram nodes and trace annotations use the node radius. Circular step markers encode an actual processing sequence. Route arrowheads are separate for each edge and follow measured node positions.

## Components

### Buttons and inputs

Native buttons and fields keep their semantics. Primary actions use cobalt; secondary actions use a transparent background and cobalt border. The copy action reverses to white on the dark command panel and uses pale blue on hover.

Controls are at least 44px high where the layout permits. Checkbox and radio labels enlarge their activation area. The shared focus ring uses safety amber (3px, offset 4px). Native disabled states remain visible.

### Navigation and status

Active navigation reverses to a white background with cobalt text. On narrow screens, links wrap instead of disappearing behind an extra menu. Status labels contain useful state text, not decorative heading prefixes.

### System map and trace

Map selection changes the adjacent annotation without moving focus. The current trace step has a filled marker and an explicit current-state attribute. Playback is reversible, pauses on demand, and stops when the tab is hidden.

The short trace highlight and measured-bar transitions use the same exponential ease-out curve. Reduced motion disables transitions and animation. No animation implies live activity.

### Reading surfaces

White panels group related map, trace, and chart content. Long operational explanations use native expandable sections rather than modal dialogs. Code remains selectable if clipboard access fails.

## Do's and Don'ts

### Do:
- **Do** keep status text explicit and distinguish simulation from recorded evidence.
- **Do** preserve native keyboard operation and visible focus.
- **Do** keep route geometry tied to actual component positions.

### Don't:
- **Don't** turn snapshot measurements into live health indicators.
- **Don't** add external assets or connections to this offline reference.
- **Don't** import fake paper, glow, or a generic metrics-dashboard opening.

> **A local-first, event-driven runtime for ambient AI.**
> Pronounced **“murmur.”**

mrmr is an open-source runtime for connecting the events happening around you to AI-driven interpretation, deterministic policy, notifications, actions, and more capable agents.

The core idea is simple:

```text
                 ┌→ ignore
                 ├→ notify
event → interpret├→ act
                 └→ delegate
```

Most AI systems wait for a human to ask them to do something. mrmr flips that model around.

Instead of:

```text
human → prompt → agent → tools → result
```

mrmr is built around:

```text
event → interpretation → policy → outcome
```

The environment produces events. Cheap, fast models interpret what those events mean. Deterministic policy decides what is allowed to happen. More capable agents wake up only when something actually deserves them.

---

## Project thesis

Modern AI tooling is extremely good at **interactive work**:

- chat
- coding
- research
- tool use
- multi-agent execution

What is still awkward is **background intelligence**.

A new email arrives. A GitHub issue is opened. A meeting moves. A server disappears. An MQTT sensor reports something unusual. A new task is created. A document changes.

Most of these events do not require a heavyweight agent.

They require a lightweight semantic judgment:

- Does this matter?
- What kind of event is this?
- Does a human need to know?
- Can a deterministic action handle it?
- Should a more capable agent be delegated the work?

mrmr exists to provide that layer.

> **Agents should not have to run continuously. Your environment should produce events, cheap models should interpret them, deterministic policy should govern them, and capable agents should wake up only when necessary.**

---

# Core model

mrmr has six core concepts:

```text
Source
Event
Interpreter
Decision
Policy
Outcome
```

The execution path is:

```text
Source
  ↓
Event
  ↓
Filter
  ↓
Interpreter
  ↓
Decision
  ↓
Policy
  ↓
Ignore / Notify / Act / Delegate
```

## 1. Source

A **Source** detects that something happened and emits a normalized event.

Examples:

- generic webhook
- GitHub webhook
- Jira webhook
- Gmail poller
- Google Calendar poller
- RSS poller
- cron
- filesystem watcher
- MQTT subscriber
- Tailscale watcher
- HTTP endpoint
- local process
- custom plugin

Sources should be deliberately dumb.

A Gmail source should not decide whether an email matters. It should only detect new mail and emit an event.

```text
connectors produce events
interpreters understand events
policies govern outcomes
```

---

## 2. Event

Every source emits the same normalized event shape.

Example:

```json
{
  "id": "evt_01JXYZ",
  "type": "github.issue.opened",
  "source": "github",
  "timestamp": "2026-08-12T19:15:03-05:00",
  "subject": "heath0xff/mrmr#42",
  "data": {
    "title": "Add Telegram notifications",
    "body": "...",
    "author": "example-user"
  },
  "metadata": {
    "source_event_id": "123456"
  }
}
```

The runtime should make as few assumptions as possible about `data`.

The important fields are:

```text
id
type
source
timestamp
subject
data
metadata
```

Delivery is at-least-once in practice: webhooks retry, pollers can overlap.
`metadata.source_event_id` is therefore a dedup key: events are unique on
`(source, source_event_id)` (hash the payload when a source provides no id).
Duplicates are recorded and dropped, not silently discarded — they appear in
traces as `duplicate`.

Time discipline: all internal timestamps are UTC; `timestamp` carries the
source's original offset if it has one. Events persist both event time and
processing time — windowed filters and staleness rules depend on the
distinction.

---

## 3. Filter

Filters are deterministic checks that happen before invoking a model.

Examples:

```yaml
filter:
  - field: data.author
    op: neq
    value: dependabot[bot]
```

Or:

```yaml
filter:
  script: |
    return event.data.size_bytes < 500000
```

The goal is simple:

> Do not spend inference on things normal software can already decide.

Windowed conditions for sensor-like sources:

Point-in-time checks are not enough when a source emits continuously — a
people detector fires 30 boxes/second, a motion sensor emits state changes,
not arrivals. Two rules keep this sane:

- **Collapse in the source adapter.** Debounce, dwell windows, per-subject
  cooldowns, and confidence thresholds run before an Event is persisted.
  Most raw readings must never become Events at all; SQLite and the trace
  log depend on this.
- **Windowed filters in flows** for cross-event conditions that survive
  collapsing:

  ```yaml
  filter:
    - window: 60s
      min_count: 3
      match:
        type: camera.*.person_detected
    - since_last:
        type: motion.any
        longer_than: 10m
  ```

> **Ambient AI, without the ambient chaos.**

Technical description:

> **mrmr is a local-first event runtime that uses AI to decide what deserves attention, action, or an agent.**

---

# Open-source philosophy

The project should be:

```text
local-first
self-hosted
model-agnostic
agent-agnostic
hackable
observable
permissioned
boring where possible
```

Users should bring:

```text
their own models
their own agents
their own infrastructure
their own credentials
their own policies
```

mrmr provides the substrate that connects them.

---

# The invariant

If the project becomes complicated, come back to this:

```text
                 ┌→ ignore
                 ├→ notify
event → interpret├→ act

```

If a feature does not make that loop more useful, safer, easier to inspect, or easier to extend, it probably does not belong in the core.

## Read-only dashboard

With `mrmr run` active, open **http://localhost:4242/dashboard/** (use your configured port).
The HTML, CSS, and JavaScript are embedded in the Go binary. No frontend service,
build tool, external asset, or new configuration is needed.

For a remote daemon, keep its listener on loopback and use an SSH tunnel:

```sh
ssh -N -L 127.0.0.1:14242:127.0.0.1:4242 YOUR_HOST
# Open http://127.0.0.1:14242/dashboard/
```

The dashboard and its read endpoints require both a loopback peer and a local
Host header, even when the ingestion listener binds more broadly. Proxy headers
do not bypass this check. Do not expose or proxy the unauthenticated ingestion
API to make the dashboard reachable.

The page refreshes every 10 seconds while visible and shows:
- Runtime response timestamp and process start time, with a stale-data warning on failure.
- Source scope and the current process's last started, finished, and successful poll.
  Empty successful polls count. Cursor age alone is not a health signal. Polls
  that exceed three intervals (at least 30 seconds) are marked overdue, not dead.
  A source can complete a batch while individual model calls fail.
- Searchable events in 50-row pages, with separate decision and execution states,
  unlabeled/error/shadow filters, and full event inspection.
- Exact repeated messages in the latest 1,000 events, without classifying them
  as harmless. Summary messages are shortened after redaction.
- Configured policy conditions and shadow boundaries, without effect arguments.

**Latency:** every Decision already stores `latency_ms` in SQLite, including
failures. A payload-free service log now records that timing for API and source
events alike. It sums client-side model requests across attempts, including
network/server time but excluding retry waits and the rest of the pipeline.
It is **not GPU-only inference time**. The dashboard groups the latest 1,000
Decisions across all models by interpreter and exact model identity. Median and
p95 use successful Decisions only, with nearest-rank percentiles. Failures remain
visible separately; timeout counts use recorded timeout/deadline error text and
count Decisions, not attempts. Historical records work without replay or new
model calls. No samples means unknown, not zero.

The latest recorded success does not prove that a model is reachable now.
Poll health resets on process restart; historical poll failures are not stored
by this view. A dashboard served by mrmr cannot independently alert when mrmr
is down.

Read endpoints: `GET /dashboard/api/overview`,
`GET /dashboard/api/events?q=TEXT&view=all&offset=0`, and
`GET /dashboard/api/event?id=EVENT_ID`. Views are `all`, `unlabeled`,
`shadow`, `ignore`, and `errors`. Queries have a five-second context deadline;
responses are capped at 4 MiB. Event detail includes `event_json`, a redacted
display string that preserves large JSON numbers without browser rounding.

# Local web UI

## Implemented read-only slice

The Go binary serves `/dashboard/` with live read-only endpoints. It shows
source-poll health, configured collection scope, event search and inspection,
shadow policy boundaries, repeated messages, and model request latency.
Decision latency remains in SQLite; payload-free timing logs cover every source.
Median/p95 use successful decisions in a bounded recent window; failures are
reported separately. Client request time is not GPU-only inference time.

Dashboard access is loopback-only, including when the ingestion listener binds
more broadly. Remote access uses an SSH tunnel. It cannot change configuration,
labels, effects, or services. Poll health is process-local; the browser shows
stale data on refresh failure. This is visibility, not independent monitoring.
The flow editor, connection manager, and control surfaces below remain future work.

## Design direction

mrmr should ship with a local web interface.

The first version should avoid becoming an enormous visual-programming IDE.

Start with four areas:

```text
Flows
Events
Agents
Connections
```

edits.newText:
The dashboard requires a loopback peer and a local Host header by default,
even when the ingestion listener binds more broadly. Proxy headers do not
bypass this check. Do not expose or proxy the unauthenticated ingestion API.

For private HTTPS through **Tailscale Serve**, configure a separate read-only
listener in the same process. Replace the hostname with your node's exact
Tailscale DNS name; both settings are required:

```yaml
server:
  addr: 127.0.0.1:4242
  dashboard_addr: 127.0.0.1:4244
  dashboard_host: your-host.your-tailnet.ts.net
```

`dashboard_addr` must use a literal loopback IP and a nonzero port.
`dashboard_host` adds one exact hostname to the Host allowlist; it does not
permit remote socket peers, arbitrary proxy headers, or cross-origin reads.
Restart mrmr after changing configuration. On that same host, inspect existing
Serve routes, then add only the dashboard route:

```sh
tailscale serve status
tailscale serve --bg --set-path=/dashboard/ http://127.0.0.1:4244/dashboard/
# Open https://your-host.your-tailnet.ts.net/dashboard/
```

Keep existing routes intact. Never enable Funnel. The second listener has no
event-ingestion routes, even if a proxy rewrites paths. Access follows existing
tailnet permissions for the node's HTTPS port; the dashboard adds no separate
sign-in. Restrict those permissions if other tailnet users must not read events.

# Dashboard — private HTTPS on Marvin

[Wiki home](README.md)

Open **https://marvin.tail91529e.ts.net/dashboard/** while connected to Tailscale.
No SSH tunnel is needed. The runtime and its database remain on Marvin.

## Access boundary

- Tailscale Serve proxies `/dashboard/` to `http://127.0.0.1:4244/dashboard/`.
- Port 4244 serves only the read-only dashboard. It has no ingestion handler.
- The existing ingestion listener stays on `127.0.0.1:4242`.
- The existing Rex route, `/` → `unix:/run/rex/serve.sock`, is unchanged.
- Funnel is not enabled. No public listener or tailnet ACL change was made.
- Existing permissions for Marvin's HTTPS port control dashboard access. There
  is no extra application sign-in. Event text can contain private information.

The configuration gained only these fields under `server`:

```yaml
dashboard_addr: 127.0.0.1:4244
dashboard_host: marvin.tail91529e.ts.net
```

The dashboard still requires a loopback socket peer. It accepts the explicit
proxy hostname but does not trust forwarded headers to grant access. Host,
Origin, and cross-site checks remain active.

## Deployment and checks — 2026-10-26

The HTTPS and visual update was installed at about 02:30 UTC. Only the
`mrmr-shadow.service` user service was stopped and started. The unit file,
sources, model settings, and shadow policy stayed unchanged. No synthetic event,
model call, or notification was sent for verification.

Current executable SHA256:

```text
0da71545413ec01f0fa2ca9dcf71e5e4e2c0ec0640b9d2dcf18f81630c75db47
```

Built from `edd8ce1` plus the reviewed, uncommitted changes. No commit or push
was made.

Verified:

- Go tests, build, vet, targeted race tests, and Linux cross-build.
- Native configuration validation against a private database copy.
- SQLite integrity and all 36 Events, 36 Decisions, 36 Executions, and zero
  labels preserved. No new schema migration in this update; schema remains 8.
- Repeated successful journal polls after startup.
- Private HTTPS assets, overview, event list, event detail, and refresh.
- Desktop and phone browser checks with real records; no JavaScript errors.
- Synthetic browser checks at 320, 390, 768, 1024, and 1440px, including search,
  filters, pagination, stale data, recovery, exact numbers, and hostile text.
- The read-only listener rejects ingestion. The HTTPS dashboard rejects POST;
  the existing root route returns 404 for `/api/events`.
- Serve configuration differs only by the added dashboard route.
- Plex, LFM2.5, Tailscale, SSH socket, and Hermes remained active.

The design keeps the cobalt identity. It adds Marvin's hostname, a clearer
information hierarchy, compact evidence summaries, explicit shadow/error
states, and complete event/latency records on phones. Detailed measurement and
source explanations remain available in expandable sections.

At verification, historical successful request latency had a **61 ms median**
and **142 ms p95**, with 33 successful Decisions and three timeouts. These counts
include synthetic checks. They are not a new benchmark or GPU-only timings.

## Backup and recovery

Current update backup:

```text
/home/heath/mrmr-shadow/rollback/dashboard-https-20261026T022931Z/
```

Contains the previous binary/configuration/unit, `serve-before.json`, a final
stopped-process database backup, and `manifest.json` with hashes and checks.
`validation.db` and `validation.yaml` were used for preflight only.

To remove only this route, preserve Rex and use:

```sh
sudo tailscale serve --https=443 --set-path=/dashboard/ off
```

Do not use `serve reset` or disable the whole HTTPS server. A binary rollback
must restore the matching configuration while mrmr is stopped. The immediately
previous binary also supports schema 8, so do not replace the live database with
an old backup and lose later events.

The original dashboard installation at about 02:03 UTC added schema 8 indexes.
Its older backup remains at:

```text
/home/heath/mrmr-shadow/rollback/dashboard-20261026T020158Z-k7r0ging/
```

Do not run that backup's pre-dashboard binary against schema 8.

## SSH fallback

If private HTTPS is unavailable, start a foreground tunnel:

```sh
ssh -N -L 127.0.0.1:14242:127.0.0.1:4244 marvin
# Open http://127.0.0.1:14242/dashboard/
```

The previous background tunnel was closed after HTTPS passed verification.

## Remaining limits

This dashboard cannot alert independently when mrmr is down. Poll health resets
on restart; old model successes do not prove current availability. No new real
event arrived during verification, so a post-upgrade decision-timing log line
remains unverified. No synthetic record was added to force one.

# Read-only runtime dashboard

Mode: Operate. Heath approved the proposed first version: live runtime and source
visibility, collection scope, searchable event history, event traces, review
status, and repeated messages. He also requested d1 latency logging. No editor,
service controls, public listener, or live-effect promotion is in scope.

It borrows the existing atlas palette, native controls, and reading fonts. The
atlas itself stays an offline snapshot. The dashboard is served by the running
Go process; it is not a replacement for independent monitoring.

## Direction contract

THESIS: Separate a quiet source from a stopped collector, and show the evidence
behind each model judgment and intended effect.

OWN-WORLD: Existing cobalt, cool paper, white tables, ink, and amber. Charter with
Georgia fallback for the main heading; system sans for controls and reading;
monospace only for JSON. Green denotes a recorded success and red a recorded
failure, always with text. These status additions are local to this surface.

STORY: Read freshness and source status; inspect request latency; search events;
open one event to see the message, decision, outcome, and trace. Check selected
units and shadow rules without changing them.

FIRST VIEWPORT: A compact masthead and evidence banner, inline totals and source
status, then latency and the start of the event timeline. Collection scope sits
alongside on desktop and below the bounded timeline on mobile.

FORM: A read-only activity table with an inline detail section. No modal, chart
costume, external assets, or animation implying live activity. Keyboard focus and
expanded source/policy details survive automatic refresh.

# Local web UI

## Implemented read-only slice

The Go binary serves `/dashboard/` with live read-only endpoints. It shows
source-poll health, configured collection scope, event search and inspection,
shadow policy boundaries, repeated messages, and model request latency.
Decision latency remains in SQLite; payload-free timing logs cover every source.
Median/p95 use successful decisions in a bounded recent window; failures are
reported separately. Client request time is not GPU-only inference time.

Dashboard socket access is loopback-only, including when the ingestion listener
binds more broadly. Remote access uses an SSH tunnel or private Tailscale Serve.
Optional `server.dashboard_addr` and `server.dashboard_host` settings add a
separate loopback-only, read-only listener and one exact trusted proxy hostname.
The proxy must target this listener, never the event-ingestion listener. Existing
tailnet permissions control remote access; forwarded headers grant no authority.
The dashboard cannot change configuration, labels, effects, or services. Poll
health is process-local; the browser shows stale data on refresh failure. This
is visibility, not independent monitoring.
The flow editor, connection manager, and control surfaces below remain future work.
